sec.title: Background
sec.p: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is highly malignant with a poor prognosis. Current treatment methods fail to prolong patients’ survival periods, and there is an urgent need to explore new strategies. EZH2 is highly expressed in ATC, and its inhibitors EPZ6438 and GSK343 have anti-cancer potential. However, issues such as insufficient drug concentration at the tumor site, drug resistance, and toxic side effects exist. Bovine serum albumin-chitosan nanoparticles have good biocompatibility, can be slowly degraded, continuously release drugs, and enable targeted drug delivery. This study used bovine serum albumin and chitosan as raw materials to prepare nano-delivery devices loaded with GSK343 and EPZ6438, providing new ideas for clinical treatment.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Two types of nanoparticles were constructed using self-assembly technology, and their characterization and drug release rates were verified. The blood compatibility, in vitro uptake, and effects on the proliferation and apoptosis of ATC cells of the nanoparticles were detected through multiple experiments. Model mice were constructed to explore the in vivo targeting and anti-tumor activity of the nanoparticles and evaluate their biosafety and effectiveness.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Two types of nanoparticles were successfully prepared with good characterization, high drug loading capacity, and encapsulation efficiency, and exhibited a sustained-release effect. In vitro experiments showed that the drug-loaded nanoparticles could induce cancer cell apoptosis and inhibit migration and invasion. In vivo studies confirmed that the nanoparticles could inhibit cell metastasis and had excellent biosafety.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Two types of nanoparticles were successfully constructed with good sustained-release, targeting effects, and biosafety. They could improve the therapeutic efficacy and reduce toxic side effects, with GSK343-BSA@CS showing significant effects.

sec.title: Key findings
sec.p: • Using bovine serum albumin (BSA) and chitosan (CS) as raw materials, prepare a nano-delivery system loaded with GSK343 or EPZ6438, increasing the accumulation of the drug in tumor sites, improving bioavailability, enabling it to better exert its therapeutic effects, reducing toxic side effects, and providing a new approach and method for the clinical treatment of anaplastic thyroid carcinoma.

sec.title: What is known and what is new?
sec.p: • Most anti-tumor drugs generally have problems such as insufficient chemical stability, significant toxic side effects, lack of tumor targeting, and overly rapid metabolism in systemic circulation, resulting in the need for the drugs to rely on systemic administration to achieve limited accumulation at the tumor site.

• Using natural compounds BSA and CS to load EZH2 inhibitors to synthesize a nano drug delivery device, allowing the EZH2 inhibitors to accumulate at the tumor site for a long time, reducing side effects, increasing efficacy, and achieving the effect of inhibiting tumor growth.

sec.title: What is the implication, and what should change now?
sec.p: • Nanomedicine delivery devices have great potential in cancer research.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Thyroid carcinoma represents the most prevalent malignant neoplasm within the endocrine system, with a notable increase in its incidence rate observed over recent years (1). Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is a rare and highly aggressive subtype of thyroid cancer, characterized by a poor prognosis and frequently associated with both local and distant metastases. The median survival time for affected patients is limited to 3 to 7 months (2). Currently, no established therapeutic interventions are capable of significantly prolonging (3).

Recent studies have underscored that many anticancer agents face common challenges, including suboptimal stability, insufficient tumor specificity, and rapid elimination from the body. These issues considerably hinder the safe and effective delivery of these agents to tumor sites via systemic administration. In response to these challenges, various drug delivery systems have been developed to enhance the therapeutic efficacy of anticancer drugs by focusing on preserving their circulation within the bloodstream and improving their bioavailability. Nanoparticles are emerging as promising vectors for delivering anti-cancer therapeutics due to their ability to facilitate controlled release while selectively targeting tumor tissues (4). The implementation of efficient and regulated drug delivery systems—particularly those utilizing nature-derived nanoparticle platforms—aims to mitigate premature release of anticancer compounds. Such systems promote preferential accumulation of bioactive agents within solid tumor microenvironments (5). Bovine serum albumin (BSA) is widely utilized in drug delivery systems for hydrophobic anticancer agents due to its negligible cytotoxicity, effectiveness in reducing nonspecific interactions, and favorable biocompatibility profile. Albumin is a high-molecular-weight protein known for its enhanced permeability and efficacy related to the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect. Research has shown that the nanoparticle formulation of paclitaxel bound to albumin, referred to as Abraxane, demonstrates superior therapeutic efficacy compared to conventional paclitaxel preparations in treating inoperable pancreatic cancer. This increased efficacy can be attributed to the transport mechanism of Abraxane, which utilizes the albumin receptor Gp60 located on the luminal surface of vascular endothelial cells. As a result, albumin is selectively and actively directed toward tumor cells through interaction with this receptor (6). Studies indicate that cancerous cells actively promote the uptake of albumin as a source of essential amino acids (7). Furthermore, it has been observed that albumin accumulates within tumor microenvironments—a phenomenon resulting from leakage from compromised vascular networks and impaired lymphatic drainage (8). Chitosan (CS) is synthesized via partial deacetylation of chitin, a marine biopolymer, under stringent alkaline conditions (9). CS represents an exceptional natural biopolymer characterized by outstanding biocompatibility and biodegradability properties; thus, it has found extensive applications within the pharmaceutical sector. CS nanoparticles represent a promising carrier for delivering anti-cancer drugs. They can encapsulate hydrophobic molecules to enhance their solubility and other properties, achieving solubilization without the need for surfactants. This approach can increase drug concentration at tumor sites, prevent toxicity caused by surfactants, and potentially circumvent drug resistance. Additionally, CS nanoparticles can slowly release anti-cancer agents, making treatment more effective and reducing the frequency of drug administration. Hypoxia-responsive CS-based nanoparticles can precisely deliver fingolimod to the core of triple-negative breast cancer tumors, significantly enhancing therapeutic efficacy while minimizing side effects (10,11).

EZH2 functions as the primary catalytic subunit of the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), which also includes EED, SUZ12, and the RbAp46/48 proteins. PRC2 catalyzes the methylation of lysine residue 27 on histone H3 (H3K27), leading to enhanced chromatin condensation and subsequent gene expression silencing (12,13). EZH2, a histone-lysine methyltransferase, is overexpressed in various malignant tumors, including those of the head and neck, bladder, colorectal region, and non-small cell lung cancers. This overexpression is significantly associated with poor prognostic outcomes. The elevated levels of EZH2 have been linked to the aggressive progression observed in these cancer types (12). EZH2 plays a crucial role in the proliferation of diverse cancer cell lines; its methyltransferase domain is essential for sustaining this process (14). Mutations in EZH2 lead to dysregulation of H3K27 trimethylation, which subsequently suppresses the expression of genes targeted by the polycomb repressive complex. The recognition of EZH2 enzyme functionality as a key driver in carcinogenesis has generated considerable interest in developing targeted inhibitors. EZH2 inhibitors have garnered widespread attention in the research field (15). EZH2 is an important therapeutic target for many malignant tumors (16). For example, initial findings indicate that two EZH2 inhibitors—GSK343 and EPZ6438—show promise in treating diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and follicular lymphoma (17,18). EPZ6438, a derivative of hemacetamipodate that acts as an EZH2 inhibitor, has been clinically employed for the treatment of inoperable epithelial-like sarcomas. It is noteworthy that EPZ6438 was the first EZH2 inhibitor to receive approval from the United States Food and Drug Administration in 2020 for therapeutic applications (19). GSK343 has been shown to effectively inhibit the enzymatic activity of EZH2, leading to a reduction in the proliferation of various cancer cell lines, including those originating from ovarian cancer (20), osteosarcoma (21), neuroblastoma and glioma (22). Additionally, it enhances the processes of programmed cell death and autophagy (23). In light of the differing efficacies observed for EPZ6438 and GSK343 in clinical trials, we undertook a study to explore the distinct effects of nanoparticle-encapsulated formulations of these two inhibitors on ATC cells. In this study, we developed a nanoscale drug delivery system, referred to as BSA@CS, aimed at improving drug accumulation at the tumor site, thereby effectively inhibiting tumor proliferation and slowing the progression of cancer metastasis. We present this article in accordance with the MDAR and ARRIVE reporting checklists (available at https://tcr.amegroups.com/article/view/10.21037/tcr-2025-aw-2433/rc).

sec.title: Materials
sec.p: EZH2 inhibitors, GSK343 and EPZ6438, were procured from TargetMol (Taoshu Biotechnology, Shanghai, China). BSA was sourced from Beijing Coolabio Technology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). CS was acquired from Sigma-Aldrich Merck, St. Louis, USA. The thyroid undifferentiated cancer cell line 8305C was obtained from Wuhan Pnuosai Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Wuhan, China), while the normal thyroid cell line Nthy-ori 3-1 was purchased from Suzhou Haixing Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Suzhou, China). RPMI-1640 and MEM (supplemented with NEAA) cell culture media were obtained from Wuhan Pronose Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Wuhan, China). Fetal bovine serum was purchased from Zhejiang Tianhang Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Huzhou, China). Coumarin-6 was sourced from Shanghai Yuanye Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China), and crystal violet was obtained from Beijing Coolabio Technology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). CCK-8 reagen was procured from TargetMol. The principal investigator acquired the Annexin-V/FITC apoptosis kit from Nanjing Keygen Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Nanjing, China). The reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) kit was purchased from Tiangen Biotech Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China), and the primers used were synthesized by Sangon Biotech Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). All reagents and solvents utilized in this study were of analytical grade and were employed without further purification.

sec.title: Preparation of nanoparticles
sec.p: Add 50 mg of BSA and 10 mmol of the inhibitors GSK343 or EPZ6438 to 5 mL of ultrapure water. Place this mixture in a 150 mL Erlenmeyer flask, and using a burette, add 20 mL of absolute ethanol at a constant rate while stirring overnight on a magnetic stirrer. To prepare the CS solution, combine 200 µL of a 1% acetic acid solution with 19.8 mL of ultrapure water, then add 20 mg of CS. The resulting CS solution should be added dropwise into the BSA solution via the burette at a consistent speed. Subsequently, slowly introduce an additional 20 mL of absolute ethanol while stirring for approximately eight hours until a white solution is obtained. Centrifuge the mixture at 12,000 r/min for twenty minutes to collect the white precipitate, which consists of BSA-chitosan nanoparticles loaded with inhibitors. Afterward, freeze the product in an ultra-low temperature freezer set to −80 ℃ for twelve hours before lyophilizing it in a freeze dryer for future use. The content of GSK343 in GSK343-BSA@CS was determined using ultraviolet spectrophotometry. A standard calibration curve was constructed by measuring the absorbance of various concentrations of GSK343 (7.81–125 µg/mL) in absolute ethanol. The concentration of GSK343 in the dialysate was subsequently determined by measuring absorbance at 306 nm and interpolating from the standard curve. A parallel procedure was employed to quantify EPZ6438 in EPZ6438-BSA@CS. DL and encapsulation efficiency (EE) were calculated based on the experimentally determined drug content using established formulas.

sec.title: Characterization of nanoparticles
sec.p: The morphological characteristics of the nanoparticles were elucidated through transmission electron microscopy analysis. The specimens were treated with a 2% phosphotungstic acid solution, subsequently dried, and analyzed using a JEOL JEM-1200 EX transmission electron microscope manufactured by JEOL Ltd., Japan. The hydrodynamic diameter, zeta potential, and polydispersity index of the MBMC LF were quantified utilizing the Nicomp-380 ZLS particle size analyzer. UV-Vis spectroscopic analysis and DL determination were performed using the UV-3802 spectrophotometer produced by Unicosh based in Shanghai. Fourier Transform Infrared (FT-IR) spectra for MBMC were obtained employing an Agilent 1260 Fourier Transform Infrared Spectrometer manufactured by Thermo Scientific, headquartered in the United States. In vitro studies demonstrated the release of the inhibitor through dialysis experiments. Drug-encapsulated nanoparticles were introduced into a dialysis membrane tube, which was then submerged in a 30.0 mL volume of PBS solution at pH 5.5, supplemented with 2% SDS. The tube was agitated at a constant rate of 100 rpm within an incubator set to maintain a temperature of 37 ℃. At designated intervals, 1.0 mL samples of the release medium were withdrawn and replaced with an equal volume (1.0 mL) of fresh release medium to maintain system consistency. Sample analyses were conducted utilizing a UV detector set at a wavelength of 294 nm integrated with the UPLC Watts technological platform.

sec.title: Cell culture
sec.p: The 8305C cell line was maintained in MEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and 1% penicillin-streptomycin. The cells were incubated in a humidified environment at 37 ℃ with an atmosphere containing 5% CO2.

sec.title: Flow cytometry analysis
sec.p: Flow cytometric analysis was utilized to quantify the fluorescence absorption characteristics of the modified Cou6 nanoparticles. The 8305C cell line was cultured in medium-sized dishes at a seeding density of 7×105 cells per dish. Following a 24-hour incubation period at 37 ℃, the cells were rinsed with PBS. Subsequently, 2.0 mL of serum-free MEM medium, supplemented with either free Cou6 or Cou6-BSA@CS at a final concentration of 100 ng/mL for Cou6, was added to each dish. After an additional incubation period of 3 hours at 37 ℃, the cells were harvested and PBS was introduced before transferring the samples to flow cytometry tubes for subsequent analysis. The fluorescence intensity of Cou6 was quantified across different treatment groups using a FACScan flow cytometer (Becton Dickinson, Franklin Lakes, USA).

sec.title: Laser confocal microscope analysis
sec.p: The distribution patterns of Cou6 and Cou6-BSA@CS within 8305C cells were analyzed using laser confocal microscopy. 8305C cells were cultured in glass Petri dishes at a density of 1×105 cells per well. After a 24-hour incubation at 37 ℃, the cells were washed with PBS. Subsequently, 2.0 mL aliquots of free Cou6 and Cou6-BSA@CS, each suspended in serum-free MEM medium, were added to the wells, resulting in a final concentration of 100 ng/mL. Following a 3-hour incubation at 37 ℃, the cells were washed with chilled PBS, fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, and stained with Hoechst 33258 dye. Fluorescence microscopy images were acquired using a Nikon confocal laser microscope, manufactured in Japan, to ensure high-resolution and detailed visualization of the samples.

sec.title: In vitro cytotoxicity test
sec.p: The cytotoxic effects of drug-encapsulated nanoparticles, unmodified nanoparticles, and free drug formulations were evaluated against the 8305C cell line using the CCK-8 assay. In these experiments, 8305C cells were cultured in 96-well plates at a density of 4×103 cells per well and incubated at 37 ℃ for 24 hours. Following this incubation period, the cells were treated with GSK343-BSA@CS, EPZ6438-BSA@CS, BSA@CS, as well as free GSK343 and EPZ6438 solutions for 36 hours. After the treatment, Remove the original culture medium and add 100 µL of basal culture medium to each well, the CCK-8 reagent was added to each sample, and the samples were incubated in a cell culture incubator for 60 minutes. The optical density (OD) of the absorbance was then measured at a wavelength of 450 nanometers using a microplate reader.

sec.title: In vitro cell apoptosis experiment
sec.p: Logarithmically growing 8305C cells were seeded into 60 mm cell culture dishes at a density of 7×105 cells per dish and cultured for 12 h. Then, culture medium solutions containing BSA@CS, GSK343, EPZ6438, GSK343-BSA@CS, and EPZ6438-BSA@CS were added to each dish respectively. After 48 h of drug treatment, the cells were collected. One mL of pre-chilled PBS buffer was added to resuspend the cells. After centrifugation, the supernatant was discarded (this operation was repeated twice). Subsequently, 200 µL of Binding Buffer was added to resuspend the cells. Then, 5 µL of Annexin V-FITC and 10 µL of PI were added respectively for staining, and the mixture was thoroughly mixed. After that, the samples were placed in a light-protected environment and incubated at room temperature for 15 min. Next, an additional 200 µL of Binding Buffer was added. Finally, the apoptotic status of the cells was detected using a flow cytometer.

sec.title: Cell migration and invasion assay
sec.p: In the scratch wound healing assay, a consistent horizontal line was marked across the bottom of a six-well plate using a marking pen. Following this, 8305C cells were plated at a density of 3.5×105 cells per well and incubated for 24 hours to reach approximately 80% confluence. A vertical scratch was then created using a pipette tip, oriented perpendicularly to the well plate. The culture medium was subsequently removed and replaced with PBS, allowing for the visualization of cell migration at the initial time point (0 hours) using an inverted Zeiss microscope (Axio Observer A1). Thereafter, drug-encapsulated nanoparticles, uncoated nanoparticles, and a free drug solution were added to the wells in MEM containing 2% FBS. Cell migration was monitored over a 24-hour period using the same inverted microscope.

sec.title: RT-qPCR
sec.p: In accordance with the manufacturer’s guidelines, total RNA was extracted from 8305C cells utilizing Trizol reagent, followed by reverse transcription employing a reverse transcription kit. In this experiment, we measured cDNA concentration with a spectrophotometer and adjusted it to 50 ng/µL. Each 20 µL reaction system contained 10 µL SYBR Green Premix Ex Taq™, 0.5 µL forward primer (10 µM), 0.5 µL reverse primer (10 µM), 2 µL cDNA template, and 7 µL nuclease-free water. Cycling conditions: 95 ℃ pre-denaturation for 30 s; 40 cycles of 95 ℃ denaturation for 5 s, primer-specific annealing (listed in manuscript) for 30 s, and 72 ℃ extension for 30 s; finally, a melting curve analysis from 65 to 95 ℃ at 0.5 ℃/s.
We used melting curve analysis to confirm primer specificity. Following the above cycling conditions, each primer pair showed a single, sharp peak, indicating a single, specific PCR product.

To ensure the 2–ΔΔCt method’s suitability for quantitative gene expression analysis, we conducted standard curve analysis to confirm amplification efficiency. We prepared cDNA template dilutions (1:1, 1:10, 1:100, 1:1,000) and performed RT-qPCR with each primer pair. Plotting Ct values against the logarithm of the dilution factor generated a standard curve. Amplification efficiency (E) was calculated as E=10(–1/slope). All primer pairs had efficiencies within 90–110%, showing the 2–ΔΔCt method was appropriate.

Subsequently, the expression levels of the target gene were assessed through RT-qPCR using an ABI 7500 real-time PCR system (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, USA) in conjunction with FastStart Universal SYBR Green Master. The relative expressions of E-cadherin, N-cadherin, and Vimentin were analyzed using the 2−ΔΔCt method, with GAPDH serving as the endogenous control. The primer sequences utilized in this investigation are presented in Table 1.

sec.title: In vivo fluorescence imaging
sec.p: Experiments were performed under a project license (No. Qi Medical Affiliate 1 Animal Review [2024] No. 2) granted by the Animal Ethics Care Committee of Qiqihar Medical University, in compliance with Regulations for the Administration of Laboratory Animals for the care and use of animals. In this study, female BALB/c mice, aged 6 weeks and with an average weight of 18.0±1.0 g, were employed to establish a model of 8305C tumor-bearing subjects. This was achieved by administering a subcutaneous injection of 1.5×106 8305C cells into the axillary region of each mouse. Once the tumor volume reached approximately 100–200 mm3 (formula: length×width2/2), indocyanine green (ICG) and ICG-BSA@CS were administered intravenously via the tail vein. The mice were anesthetized with isoflurane at specified intervals for imaging purposes. Fluorescence imaging was performed using the IVIS Lumina Series III in vivo imaging system (Perkin Elmer, Waltham, USA) to obtain the necessary images. Following the imaging procedures, the mice were euthanized, and tumors along with major organs were excised for subsequent in vitro imaging analyses.

sec.title: Antitumor activity in vivo
sec.p: The in vivo antitumor efficacy of drug-loaded nanoparticles was evaluated using the 8305C murine tumor model. Seven days after inoculation with 8305C cells, the model mice were randomly divided into five experimental groups, with six mice in each group. GSK343-BSA@CS, EPZ6438-BSA@CS, as well as GSK343 and EPZ6438, were administered intravenously via the tail vein of the mice. The drugs were given every 48 hours at a dose of 20 mg/kg in a volume of 100 µL for 20 days. During this period, the tumor volume and body weight of the mice were monitored. After the completion of the treatment, the mice were euthanized, and the major organs and tumors were excised for further analysis. The tumor mass was quantified, and imaging techniques were employed to evaluate the efficacy of the antitumor response. Subsequently, tissue sections were prepared for histological analysis and examined using hematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining. In addition, an assessment of the biosafety implications associated with the use of nanoparticles was also conducted.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: In this study, graphing and data analysis were conducted using GraphPad Prism 9.5 and Origin 2022 software. Measurement data were presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM) or mean ± standard deviation (SD). For comparisons between two groups, a t-test was employed, while analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used for comparisons among three groups. A statistically significant difference was defined as P<0.05, indicated by an asterisk (*); P<0.01 was marked with two asterisks (**); P<0.001 with three asterisks (***); and P<0.0001 with four asterisks (****). Each experimental protocol was carried out with three independent biological replicates. For cell-based assays, each treatment group was tested in three independent biological replicates, with each replicate measured in triplicate; logical replicates (n=6 per group) were used, with each replicate representing a distinct cohort of animals housed in separate cages to minimize pseudo-replication.

sec.title: Preparation and characterization of nanoparticles
sec.p: EZH2 is highly expressed in ATC (24). Nanoparticles, distinguished by their small dimensions and high specific surface area, constitute an essential component of biomaterials. These attributes enable them to effectively navigate biological barriers, achieve targeted accumulation at specific sites, penetrate cellular membranes, and markedly improve the efficacy of anticancer drug delivery. Consequently, they have attracted significant attention within the field of drug delivery (25). In light of the findings, an EZH2 inhibitor was chosen for the formulation of nanoparticles. The nanoparticles were synthesized using BSA and CS as the primary components, which self-assembled through electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions. TEM imaging demonstrated that the drug-conjugated nanoparticles were uniformly distributed and exhibited a spherical morphology. The TEM analysis indicated that the GSK343-BSA@CS nanoparticles had an average diameter of 250±18 nm (Figure 1A), while the EPZ6438-BSA@CS nanoparticles measured an average diameter of 260±18 nm (Figure 1B). The Zeta potential of the nanoparticles was measured using a Zeta potential meter, with the results illustrated in Figure 1C. The control nanoparticles, BSA@CS, exhibited a Zeta potential of −16±0.3 mV, whereas the drug-loaded nanoparticles, GSK343-BSA@CS and EPZ6438-BSA@CS, displayed Zeta potentials of −19.8±0.3 and −19.5±0.3 mV, respectively. Dynamic light scattering was utilized to determine the hydrated particle size, with the results presented in Figure 1D-1F. The hydrated particle size for BSA@CS nanoparticles was found to be 287±10.5 nm, while GSK343-BSA@CS and EPZ6438-BSA@CS nanoparticles measured 287.7±10.3 and 287.9±11.9 nm, respectively. FTIR spectroscopy was performed to compare the spectra of BSA, CS, GSK343, and GSK343-BSA@CS. As shown in Figure 1G,1H, the infrared spectrum of the physically blended sample displayed an overlay of the primary characteristic peaks of BSA, CS, and the inhibitor. Notably, the peak in the 3,400–3,200 cm⁻1 range, which corresponds to O-H and N-H stretching and vibration, did not exhibit significant changes, indicating a simple superposition of the peaks. In the spectrum of GSK343-BSA@CS, this peak broadened and its intensity decreased, suggesting the potential formation of a hydrogen bond network. Distinct shifts in the amide C=O stretching vibration and variations in the intensity and position of the N-H bending vibration were observed, which may indicate interactions between the protein and either CS or GSK343 molecules. The C-O vibration peak of CS, located at approximately 1,100 cm⁻1, showed significant weakening or shifting, indicating involvement in chemical or physical crosslinking. These observations of peak broadening, intensity changes, and displacements suggest the formation of chemical bonds or physical crosslinking among BSA, CS, and GSK343, particularly in functional groups such as O-H, N-H, and C-O, thereby confirming the successful synthesis of GSK343-BSA@CS nanoparticles with synergistic effects. The EPZ6438-BSA@CS sample also exhibited distinct infrared characteristics, indicating the formation of chemical bonds or strong interactions, including hydrogen bonds or cross-linking networks, during the nanoparticle synthesis, which further enhances molecular synergy. The results confirm the successful synthesis of two distinct types of nanoparticles. The release kinetics of GSK343 and EPZ6438 from these nanoparticles were examined through dialysis at 37 ℃, with the release curves illustrated in Figure S1. At a pH of 5.5, the release data indicated that GSK343-BSA@CS nanoparticles attained a cumulative release rate of 73.49% over a period of 36 hours, while EPZ6438-BSA@CS nanoparticles exhibited a cumulative release rate of 69.58%. The calibration curve of GSK343 was analyzed and yielded the linear regression equation Y = 0.0261X − 0.0527 with a coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.9994. Based on this equation, the DL of GSK343 in GSK343-BSA@CS nanoparticles was determined to be 2.073%, and the encapsulation efficiency (EE) was calculated as 98.8%. For EPZ6438, the standard curve was fitted to the equation Y = 0.013X + 0.0823, with an R2 value of 0.9991. Using this calibration model, the DL in EPZ6438-BSA@CS probes was found to be 9.05%, with an encapsulation efficiency of 99.5%.

sec.title: In vitro cellular uptake
sec.p: The uptake of 8305C cells co-incubated with PBS, Cou6, and Cou6-BSA@CS was examined using confocal laser microscopy, while flow cytometry was employed for quantitative assessment. The blue fluorescence observed intracellularly was attributed to DAPI-stained nuclei, whereas the green fluorescence was derived from the Cou6 fluorescent dye (Figure 2A). The findings revealed that, although the fluorescence intensity of the free Cou6 group surpassed that of the Cou6-BSA@CS in 8305C cells, the fluorescence signal from the nanoparticle group was significantly greater than that of the control group. To further ascertain the internalization of the nanoparticles by the cells, flow cytometry was utilized to evaluate the cellular uptake of the nanoparticles (Figure 2B). The results demonstrated that the nanoparticles were capable of diffusing into cancer cells. The drugs encapsulated within the nanoparticles could enter the cancer cells via two mechanisms. The first mechanism involved the adherence of nanoparticles to the cell membrane, which established a drug concentration gradient that facilitated the gradual permeation of the drugs into the cells. The second mechanism entailed the adsorption of nanoparticles onto the cell membrane surface, followed by internalization through endocytosis, allowing for the gradual release of Cou6 from the nanocarriers within the cancer cells. Our data suggest that BSA-CS nanoparticles serve as effective drug carriers, capable of delivering high concentrations of therapeutic agents into cells, thereby enhancing the efficacy of cancer treatment.

sec.title: In vitro cytotoxicity analysis
sec.p: The evaluation of the biosafety of nanoparticles is essential for their subsequent application in in vivo studies. The cytotoxic effects of GSK343, EPZ6438, BSA@CS, GSK343-BSA@CS, and EPZ6438-BSA@CS were investigated using the CCK-8 assay. In the groups treated with GSK343 and GSK343-BSA@CS nanoparticles, a dose-dependent inhibition of 8305C cell viability was observed (refer to Figure 2C). Similarly, the EPZ6438 and EPZ6438-BSA@CS nanoparticle groups also exhibited a dose-dependent reduction in cell activity. Notably, GSK343 demonstrated a greater efficacy in inducing cell death compared to GSK343-BSA@CS nanoparticles, with relative cell viability recorded at 3.9% for the GSK343 group and 11.2% for the GSK343-BSA@CS group at the highest concentration (GSK343: 32.5 µg/mL). At the maximum concentration of EPZ6438-BSA@CS (EPZ6438: 45.8 µg/mL), the relative cell viability was 38.4% for both the EPZ6438 and EPZ6438-BSA@CS groups. The drug-loaded nanoparticles exhibited a reduced cytotoxic effect on 8305C cells compared to the free drug, likely due to the gradual release of the drug from the nanocarrier, which allows for a more controlled interaction with the cells, in contrast to the immediate interaction of the free drug. As illustrated in Figure S2, the BSA@CS nanoparticles, which were not loaded with drugs, displayed minimal toxicity towards Nthy-ori 3-1 cells, thereby underscoring the favorable biosafety profile of the materials utilized in the construction of the nanoparticles.

sec.title: Apoptosis assay of GSK-BSA@CS and EPZ6438-BSA@CS nanoparticles
sec.p: Flow cytometric analysis was utilized to evaluate the incidence of apoptosis in both drug-encapsulated nanoparticles and drug-exposed 8305C cells, analyzed separately. The cell cultures were treated with equivalent concentrations of drug-encapsulated nanoparticles, the free drug, and a vehicle control. Apoptosis rates were determined using the PI/Annexin-V/FITC apoptosis kit, as illustrated in Figure 2D,2E. In the control group, which did not receive any drug treatment, the apoptosis rate was recorded at 6.49%, slightly lower than the 9.95% observed in the group treated with blank nanoparticles. The significant biological safety of BSA and CS has been well-documented in the existing scientific literature (26). The recurrence of this observation underscores the remarkable safety profile associated with the material under investigation. The apoptosis rate in 8305C cells treated with GSK343 was recorded at 33.7%, while the rate for GSK343 encapsulated within nanoparticles was found to be 26.8%. In contrast, the apoptosis rate in 8305C cells treated with EPZ6438 was measured at 26.59%, with the corresponding rate for EPZ6438-formulated nanoparticles being 19.69%. These results suggest that both free GSK343 and its drug-encapsulated formulations exhibit a greater efficacy in inducing apoptosis compared to the EPZ6438 group. Additionally, the in vitro analysis indicates that the drug-loaded nanoparticles possess a reduced ability to induce apoptosis in 8305C cells when compared to the unencapsulated drug.

sec.title: In vitro investigation into the suppression of cellular migration and invasive capabilities
sec.p: ATC is distinguished by its pronounced metastatic potential and aggressive malignancy. This study aims to investigate the efficacy of nanoparticles in inhibiting the migration of 8305C cells and to compare the inhibitory effects of various pharmacological agents. The migratory behavior of 8305C cells was evaluated using a scratch assay, wherein cells were subjected to six different treatment conditions. The analysis of wound healing dynamics, as illustrated in Figures 3A, indicated that the control group of 8305C cells achieved a wound closure rate of 80%±3.2% at 24 hours post-injury, highlighting their significant migratory capacity and suggesting a high metastatic potential. In contrast, the healing rate for wounds treated with BSA@CS nanomaterials was recorded at 73%±3.0%, indicating that these nanomaterials did not substantially alter the cellular migration rate during the wound healing process. The most pronounced inhibitory effect on the wound healing process was observed with unbound GSK343, which resulted in a healing rate reduction to 30%±2.7%. Additionally, treatment with free EPZ6438 yielded a healing rate of 41%±2.1%. The wound healing rates for the samples treated with GSK343-BSA@CS and EPZ6438-BSA@CS were 45.5%±1.9% and 54.7%±1.5%, respectively. Notably, GSK343-BSA@CS exhibited a superior capacity for inhibiting metastasis compared to EPZ6438-BSA@CS. The effect of the inhibitor on the invasive capacity of cells was evaluated using a Matrigel-coated assay. The data presented in Figure 3B indicates that both the free drug formulations and the drug-encapsulated nanofibers significantly reduced the invasive ability of 8305C cells, as demonstrated by a notable reduction in their penetration through the Matrigel matrix in comparison to the untreated control group (Figure 3B). The application of cost-free pharmacological agents exhibited a pronounced inhibitory effect on the invasive capabilities of the cells. Notably, GSK343-BSA@CS displayed a greater efficacy in inhibiting cellular invasion relative to EPZ6438-BSA@CS. EZH2 inhibitors have been shown to possess substantial antitumor activity, particularly regarding migratory and invasive potential. In vivo comparative studies have revealed that the effectiveness of free drug formulations exceeds that of their synthetic nanoparticle equivalents. The epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is a pivotal factor in the advancement of tumor invasion and metastasis, characterized by a significant reduction in E-cadherin expression alongside an increase in the expression levels of N-cadherin and vimentin. For example, in the case of oral cancer, it combats metastasis by inhibiting EMT-mediated migration and invasion (27). During the EMT, malignant cells demonstrate a reduction in cellular adhesion, undergo morphological changes that render them similar to fibroblasts, reorganize their cytoskeletal architecture, and simultaneously enhance their abilities for migration, invasion, and metastasis (28). As illustrated in Figure 3C, all experimental groups exhibited an upregulation of E-cadherin expression, accompanied by a downregulation of vimentin and N-cadherin expression. E-cadherin serves as a marker on the surface of epithelial cells and facilitates their adhesion. The aggregated findings suggest that EZH2 acts as a pivotal regulator of EMT, effectively inhibiting the progression of tumor metastasis.

sec.p: In a comprehensive view, in vitro evaluations reveal that the free drug exhibits a more pronounced effect, while in vivo analyses indicate that the nano-drug with drug encapsulation demonstrates stronger therapeutic efficacy. There are likely three reasons for this phenomenon: firstly, tumor tissue penetration and accumulation: nanoformulations possess unique physicochemical properties, such as an appropriate particle size and surface modification, which enable them to better penetrate tumor tissues. Tumor tissues are characterized by high interstitial pressure and abnormal vascular structures. Due to its relatively small molecular weight, the free drug is prone to rapid clearance through the bloodstream and has difficulty accumulating effectively at the tumor site. In contrast, nanoformulations can enrich in tumor tissues via the EPR effect in solid tumors, achieving targeted drug delivery. This increases the drug concentration within the tumor tissue, thereby enhancing the inhibitory effect on tumor growth. Secondly, spatiotemporal control of drug release: In the complex physiological environment in vivo, nanoformulations can achieve intelligent drug release according to the characteristics of the tumor microenvironment. For instance, tumor tissues generally have a lower pH value. Some nanocarriers can be designed to rapidly release drugs in a low-pH environment, enabling precise drug release at the tumor site and improving the local efficacy of the drug. In contrast, the free drug has a relatively uniform distribution and metabolism in the body and cannot form high-concentration drug aggregates at the tumor site like nanoformulations. As a result, its inhibitory effect on tumor growth is relatively weak. Thirdly, immunomodulatory effects: nanoformulations may interact with the body’s immune system and regulate the tumor immune microenvironment. Some nanocarriers can carry immunomodulatory molecules, such as cytokines and antibodies, and co-deliver them with the drug to the tumor site. This activates the body’s immune system and enhances the ability of immune cells to recognize and kill tumor cells. In contrast, the free drug typically lacks this immunomodulatory function and has a relatively minor impact on the tumor immune microenvironment. Therefore, it may be less effective than nanoformulations in inhibiting tumor growth.

sec.title: In vivo fluorescence imaging and distribution
sec.p: Bovine serum albumin-chitosan (BSA@CS) nanoparticles labeled with ICG, as well as free ICG, were administered intravenously via the tail vein to BALB/C mice bearing 8305C tumors. The in vivo targeting efficacy of the BSA@CS nanomaterials was subsequently assessed using a real-time fluorescence imaging system. Figure 4A illustrates the in vivo fluorescence distribution patterns at various time points following the injection of ICG-BSA@CS conjugates and unbound ICG. Figure 4B presents the temporal progression of quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements across designated time intervals. The fluorescence emission from ICG-BSA@CS nanoparticles was detectable at the tumor site as early as two hours post-injection, with a notable increase in signal intensity observed at subsequent time points. The fluorescence intensity of the ICG-BSA@CS complex peaked at six hours and remained elevated for up to 24 hours. In contrast, fluorescence from free ICG at the tumor site was detectable 12 hours post-injection, although it was significantly lower than that of the ICG-BSA@CS conjugates. Following 24 hours post-injection, the mice were humanely euthanized to enable ex vivo fluorescence imaging of the tumor tissue and major organs. Ex vivo fluorescence imaging, as shown in Figure 4C,4D, indicated that the primary localization of fluorescence signals for both ICG-BSA@CS and free ICG was predominantly in the liver and kidneys. Comparative analysis revealed that ICG-BSA@CS exhibited enhanced tumor accumulation relative to free ICG, with detectable fluorescence signals present in the excised tumors. These results suggest that the BSA@CS conjugate may significantly enhance targeted drug delivery and increase drug accumulation at tumor sites.

sec.title: Antitumor effect in vivo
sec.p: To evaluate the in vivo anti-tumoral efficacy of nanoparticle-formulated pharmaceuticals, treatment regimens involving free GSK343, EPZ6438, GSK343-BSA@CS conjugates, and EPZ6438-BSA@CS conjugates were administered to BALB/C mice with subcutaneous 8305C thyroid undifferentiated carcinoma xenografts. Figure 5A-5C present a graphical representation of tumor growth kinetics following the therapeutic interventions. The data revealed that the various drug treatment groups exhibited a moderate inhibitory effect on tumor proliferation. Notably, the drug encapsulated within the nanometer formulation demonstrated significantly enhanced inhibitory effects on tumor growth compared to both the saline control and the free drug group. Among all formulations tested, the GSK343-BSA@CS nanocomplex exhibited the most pronounced tumor-inhibitory activity. The substantial inhibitory effect of the GSK343-BSA@CS group on tumor growth was corroborated by tumor mass assessments, as illustrated in Figure 5D. In comparison to the untreated group, the nano-treated group disrupted the dense structure of the tumor, leading to atrophy, degeneration, and necrosis of tumor cells, with the GSK343-BSA@CS formulation resulting in a larger necrotic area than the EPZ6438-BSA@CS formulation (Figure 5E). These results indicate that BSA-CS nanoparticles serve as an effective sustained-release system, enhancing the utilization rate of the drugs. Overall, the findings suggest that the BSA-CS nanogel demonstrates efficacy as a sustained-release system, significantly improving the bioavailability of the encapsulated pharmaceuticals.

sec.title: In vivo biological safety of nanoparticles
sec.p: Blood samples were collected from tumor-bearing mice prior to necropsy to evaluate the potential hepatotoxicity and nephrotoxicity of nanomedicines encapsulating therapeutic agents, aiming for a thorough assessment of their biological safety. The levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), urea, and creatinine were measured to assess hepatic and renal function. No significant differences in liver and kidney function markers were detected among the experimental groups (see Figure S3). Additionally, there was no notable change in the body weight of the mice throughout the treatment period (Figure 5F). Histological analysis using HE staining of key organs from mice treated with the drug-loaded nanoparticle formulation, as well as from non-tumor-bearing mice, revealed no histopathological abnormalities, such as necrosis, edema, or inflammatory cell infiltration, comparable to the control group (Figure 5F). Moreover, BSA@CS nanoparticles at concentrations up to 200 µg/mL resulted in a hemolysis rate of less than 0.5%, indicating that BSA@CS is non-hemolytic (Figure S4). Collectively, these results suggest that the developed nanoparticles do not cause organ damage and have the potential to reduce drug-related organ toxicity, thereby demonstrating improved biological safety.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In recent years, natural biomaterials—characterized by excellent biocompatibility, non-toxicity, biodegradability, and low immunogenicity—have been increasingly applied in nanomedicine research. Protein-based nanoparticles have demonstrated significant potential as drug carriers, enabling the delivery of anticancer agents, genetic material, and growth factors (29). Several such nanoparticles have already received approval from regulatory authorities, including the FDA and EMA, for use in cancer therapy (30). Among them, bovine serum BSA-CS nanoparticles are particularly promising due to their superior biocompatibility and degradability, making them effective candidates for drug delivery systems (31). However, reports on the self-assembly of CS and BSA into nanoparticles remain limited, with even fewer studies focusing on their application in drug delivery. One study developed doxorubicin-loaded CS-BSA nanoparticles and systematically evaluated their therapeutic potential in gastric cancer treatment (26). Another confirmed the feasibility of EPZ6438-loaded BSA-CS nanoparticles for osteosarcoma therapy using both in vitro cell models and in vivo subcutaneous tumor-bearing nude mice (31). Nonetheless, these investigations primarily focused on the induction of cancer cell apoptosis by BSA@CS-delivered drugs, leaving broader mechanistic insights unexplored.

In this study, we fabricated GSK343-BSA@CS and EPZ6438-BSA@CS nanoparticles through stable self-assembly driven by electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions, and further examined their efficacy in inhibiting ATC proliferation and metastasis. The resulting nanoparticles exhibited optimal nanoscale dimensions, uniform morphology, and a negative surface charge, contributing to enhanced colloidal stability and preferential accumulation at tumor sites via the EPR effect, while minimizing clearance by the reticuloendothelial system. Their in vitro and in vivo targeting capabilities were rigorously validated using laser scanning confocal microscopy, flow cytometry, and fluorescence imaging in 8305C tumor-bearing mouse models, demonstrating efficient tumor localization and prolonged retention. Notably, beyond leveraging inherent nanoparticle properties for targeting, the well-controlled nano-size enables passive targeting through the EPR effect—a phenomenon first described in 1986. Since its discovery, the EPR effect has become a cornerstone in the design of tumor-targeted nanotherapeutics, with growing emphasis on its role in preclinical development, clinical trials, and translational applications (32).

Conventional chemotherapeutic agents often induce non-specific cytotoxicity, damaging healthy tissues and rapidly dividing cells such as hematopoietic and immune cells, despite their efficacy against malignant tumors. This lack of selectivity leads to severe side effects—including nausea, vomiting, alopecia, constipation, and neurotoxicity—thereby limiting the clinical utility of traditional chemotherapy. An emerging advantage of nanocarriers lies in their ability to modulate cellular mechanobiology: during cancer progression, reduced cellular elasticity facilitates invasion and metastasis (33,34). Nanoparticles can interact with intracellular organelles and cytoskeletal components, potentially influencing cell migration, adhesion, and metastatic behavior. Moreover, nanocarriers address key limitations of conventional drugs, such as short circulation half-life, multidrug resistance, and systemic toxicity. Consequently, nanocarrier systems hold great promise for overcoming the drawbacks of free chemotherapeutics and enhancing overall therapeutic outcomes.

BSA@CS functions as a highly efficient and selective cytotoxic drug delivery platform, utilizing naturally derived, non-toxic components—albumin and CS. This composite system exhibits outstanding biocompatibility, tunable degradation kinetics, and robust structural integrity under physiological conditions, thereby minimizing immunogenic risks and toxic side effects while significantly reducing collateral damage to healthy tissues. Owing to these advantageous properties, BSA@CS is widely regarded as a highly promising vehicle for tumor-targeted therapy, particularly in improving the bioavailability and delivery efficiency of anticancer drugs (26).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This research successfully developed the GSK343-BSA@CS and EPZ6438-BSA@CS nanodrug delivery systems utilizing advanced green self-assembly technology, which ensures both high dispersibility and remarkable stability. These nanoparticles exhibit superior intracellular uptake and targeting capabilities, particularly in the context of delivering therapeutic agents to ATC cells, thereby presenting novel opportunities for cancer therapy.

The GSK343-BSA@CS and EPZ6438-BSA@CS nanoparticles not only facilitate targeted drug release but also enhance accumulation at tumor sites, significantly augmenting therapeutic efficacy. Notably, GSK343-BSA@CS nanoparticles demonstrate considerable inhibitory advantages over conventional pharmacological agents in ATC tumor models, representing a significant advancement in cancer treatment methodologies.

In addition, this nano-delivery system demonstrates favorable biocompatibility. The results of long-term toxicity evaluations indicate that it has no significant adverse effects on major organs or liver and kidney functions, thereby laying a solid foundation for potential clinical applications. In conclusion, the nano-drug delivery system for epigenetic EZH2 inhibitors developed in this study has brought certain innovations in the fields of precision medicine and cancer treatment, and is expected to provide more effective and safer therapeutic options for cancer patients.
